knowledge_type_note: Typed historical-teaching-principle rather than strategic-principle deliberately: it is Nimzowitsch's own named innovation, it is taught as his, and it is the one idea of his that later practice has been most sceptical about. Mandatory hedging applies.

attributions.note: Verified against the primary text, where he describes it as 'my innovation of overprotection'.

history.notes: Directly self-attributed in the primary text, which has been read.

development.change: Introduced as a named innovation and given its own chapter.
Retained as vocabulary but treated with scepticism in practice; the least-adopted of his ideas.

engine_era_note: The Nimzowitsch idea engines least support. They will defend a point as many times as a concrete line requires and no more, and they consistently prefer activity to redundant defence. Overprotection as a general policy does not survive; the underlying observation — that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed — does.

preconditions: A strategically important point is defended more times than it is attacked
indicators_for: The point is central and both sides want it
The overprotecting pieces are well placed for other reasons too
A blockading piece needs support from behind
indicators_against: The extra defenders have nothing else to do from those squares
The point is not under any real pressure
The tempo could be spent on something concrete
false_positive_traps: Counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing. Overprotection is a CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile, and that claim is often false.
This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well.

typical_plans: Support a blockading piece from behind
Contest a key central square with more force than the opponent
typical_piece_arrangements: Several pieces bearing on one central square
tactical_consequences: Wins the exchange sequence when the point is finally contested
strategic_consequences: Pieces in contact with a strong point are ready when lines open

exceptions: Defending an unattacked point is usually a waste of time, and modern practice says so.
Engines defend exactly as much as a line requires.
limitations: The weakest-supported concept in the Nimzowitsch cluster, and the record says so rather than presenting it at face value.
misconceptions: That overprotection is generally good practice. It is a named historical idea with limited modern support.
That more defenders is safer. Beyond what a concrete line needs, extra defenders are usually idle pieces.

examples.note: The position after 14.Nf3, annotated by Nimzowitsch himself: 'The blockading forces are to be reinforced by the knight.' This is overprotection as its author practised it — the e5 point is already held, and he adds a defender to it anyway, because the pieces that guard a strategically important square draw their own scope from doing so. Recorded here because a concept should where possible be illustrated by the player who formulated it, annotating his own move. engine.verdict_note: -0.65 at depth 22, from the side that is overprotecting. The number matters more than its sign: overprotection is a claim about durability rather than about advantage, and a record whose only example evaluated in its favour would be evidence for the wrong proposition. What is established is that the position is playable and roughly balanced with the arrangement in place.

by_level.beginner: Defending an important square more times than you strictly need to, so your pieces are ready when the fight for it comes.
by_level.intermediate: Overprotection — Nimzowitsch's idea that piling defenders on a key point is worthwhile. Treat it with care: extra defenders that do nothing else are slow moves.
by_level.advanced: His own named innovation, and the one that has aged least well. The defensible core is that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed anyway.
by_level.master: Recorded as historical teaching. Engines defend to the requirement of the line and no further.

by_depth.short: Defend a key square more times than needed.
by_depth.normal: Overprotection: Nimzowitsch's idea that defending an important point beyond necessity is worthwhile, because the defenders are well placed by their contact with a strong square and ready when it is contested.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch calls it 'my innovation' and gives it a chapter. He links it to the blockade — a blockading piece needs support from the rear — and to exchanges, since a point both sides want becomes the site of a mass liquidation the better-supported side wins. It is also the idea of his that wears worst: piling defenders onto an unattacked square looks like passivity and often is, and engines defend only as much as a concrete line requires. What survives is the narrower observation that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed for other reasons too.

explanations.hedge: A historical teaching principle and the least-supported of Nimzowitsch's ideas. Modern practice is sceptical, and engines defend a point only as many times as a concrete line requires. Do not present it as general good practice.
explanations.lesson: The idea to keep is narrower than the name: pieces aimed at a strong central square are often well placed anyway. Defending an unattacked square for its own sake is a slow move.

beginner_words: defend it more than you need to

definition_short: Defending a strategically important square or point with more pieces than are needed, so that those pieces draw strength from it.
definition_long:
Nimzowitsch calls it 'my innovation' in My System, and it is the most contested of his ideas. The claim is that piling defenders onto a key point — typically a central square — is not wasted effort, because the overprotecting pieces are themselves well placed by virtue of their contact with a strong square, and are ready when the position opens.

He ties it directly to the blockade: 'The effectiveness of the blockade is increased by links to the rear (overprotection needed!)'. And to exchanges — a strong point both sides want becomes the site of what he calls a 'great blood-letting', so the side with more defenders wins the exchange sequence.

IT IS THE IDEA OF HIS THAT WEARS WORST. Piling pieces on a square that is not under attack looks, and often is, like passivity, and modern practice is much readier to call it a waste of time. It is recorded here as a historical teaching principle rather than a live technique, with the hedge that a system that recommends overprotection without a concrete reason is recommending slow moves.
